title: The fever as a living power that Jesus rebukes
english: The Savior comes to Simon's house and finds Simon's mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. Luke writes, "Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her" (Luke 4:39). Now in the wording used by Matthew and Mark, "the fever left her" (Matthew 8:15; Mark 1:31), and in the whole account, nothing is indicated about the fever as a living creature. But in Luke's wording, "standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her," I do not know whether we are not compelled to say that the thing rebuked and leaving is a living creature that could not endure the rebuker's power. For it is not reasonable to say that something soulless and unfeeling is rebuked by a rebuke.

And it is not at all surprising that there are certain harmful powers of the human body, and we should not necessarily accuse the soul of those who suffer as though it were harmed by these things. For not even when the devil struck Job with a grievous wound, having received authority to test him through the body, should Job be accused for this. He contended and nobly endured the blow. Only let this be said, if ever we are tested through bodily pains: "but do not touch his soul" (Job 2:6), just as the Lord also heals those who are ill by rebuking. In Scripture, "He rebuked" is used in place of "he commanded."
